one_liner: Portable C++ RANLUX++ in ROOT mathcore: RANLUX-quality doubles at about 9 ns, versus 62 ns for ROOT's classic TRandom1 RANLUX.
what_it_does: Implements RANLUX++, Sibidanov's reformulation of the RANLUX subtract-with-borrow generator as an equivalent 576-bit linear congruential generator, in plain C++. You use it as ROOT::Math::RanluxppEngine24 / RanluxppEngine2048 (Rndm(), operator(), IntRndm(), SetSeed(), Skip(n)) or as the TRandom-derived TRandomRanluxpp (TRandomGen<RanluxppEngine2048>), so it replaces TRandom1 or a std::ranlux engine inside ROOT code without changing call sites. The same file also has sequence-compatible engines for James' RANLUX (p=223/389, matching gsl_rng_ranlux/ranlux389), GSL ranlxs/ranlxd, Luescher's C ranlxs/ranlxd, and std::ranlux24 / std::ranlux48.
how_it_is_fast: RANLUX normally discards hundreds of subtract-with-borrow outputs per kept block (that is its 'luxury level'); RANLUX++ instead skips p steps at once by multiplying the 576-bit state by a precomputed a^p mod m (m = 2^576 - 2^240 + 1), so a luxury level of 2048 costs one big multiply-and-reduce per block of 12 48-bit numbers. The multi-word multiply uses unsigned __int128 where the compiler has it (the blog credits this with more than 40 percent), plus fully unrolled loops via #pragma GCC unroll / #pragma unroll, branch-free overflow handling and carry propagation, and a modulo reduction that exploits the special form of m. Skip(n) is O(log n) through modular exponentiation (powermod) rather than generating and discarding.
when_to_use: You already use ROOT and want a better default than TRandom3 or TRandom1 for Monte Carlo where the generator's theoretical mixing guarantees matter (lattice QCD, detector simulation).
You currently pay for RANLUX (TRandom1, gsl_rng_ranlxd, std::ranlux48) and want the same family at a much higher luxury level (p=2048) for less time per number.

You need reproducible parallel streams: Skip(n) jumps ahead in logarithmic time through modular exponentiation, and SetSeed(s) starts at a^(s x 2^96) times a fixed initial state, so different seeds sit far apart in the same sequence.
You must stay portable (non-x86, or compilers that cannot take Sibidanov's assembly) but want close to the assembly version's speed (about 9 ns versus 8 ns in the ROOT blog).
when_not_to_use: Raw speed is the goal: in the same benchmark TRandom3 (Mersenne Twister) ran at about 3 ns per number, and xoshiro/PCG-class generators in the sibling entries are faster still.

You do not want ROOT as a dependency: the engine lives in libMathCore, derives from ROOT's TRandomEngine, and is LGPL-2.1-or-later, so extracting it means copying RanluxppEngine.h, RanluxppEngineImpl.cxx and the src/ranluxpp helper headers and stripping the base class.
Your compiler lacks unsigned __int128 (for example MSVC): mulmod.h then falls back to 32-bit partial products, and the blog attributes more than 40 percent of the tuned speed to __int128.
You need bit-for-bit continuity with ROOT 6.24.00 output: the June 2021 bias fix (PR #8293) changed the generated sequence.

integration.dependencies: ROOT (libMathCore; TRandomEngine base, TRandomGen wrapper). The ranluxpp/*.h helpers themselves need only <cstdint>.
integration.min_toolchain: C++17 (ROOT's minimum; the engine code itself uses only C++11 features). GCC 8+ or Clang for the unroll pragmas to take effect; __int128 support for full speed.
integration.platforms: any platform ROOT builds on; the helpers are portable C++ and their unroll pragmas also cover __CUDACC__ and the Intel compiler
integration.thread_safety: not documented; each engine instance holds mutable state (9 x 64-bit words, carry, bit position) without locking, so use one engine per thread
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: TRandomRanluxpp drops in wherever a TRandom (TRandom1) is used, but its sequence differs from TRandom1's; RanluxppCompatEngineJamesP3/P4 reproduce James' RANLUX sequence (gsl_rng_ranlux) and RanluxppCompatEngineStdRanlux24/48 reproduce std::ranlux24/48 sequences through ROOT's TRandomEngine interface, not the std::uniform_random_bit_generator interface.

gotchas: The 2020 timings (30 ns initial, about 9 ns tuned) were measured before the June 2021 fixes that made mod_m return the smallest representative, convert the LCG state back to RANLUX numbers on every block (to_lcg/to_ranlux), and cut output from 52 to 48 bits per double; the shipped generator has not been re-timed in a public source read here.
ROOT 6.24.00 shipped the biased version, and issue #8503 reported undefined behaviour (left shift of -1 in mulmod.h) in 6.24, fixed by PR #8522 in June 2021; use a later release.

RanluxppEngine is a pimpl (std::unique_ptr to the implementation) whose operator() is defined in the library, and TRandomRanluxpp::Rndm() is virtual, so each number pays a non-inlinable call; batch with RndmArray() where possible.
Doubles carry 48 random bits (multiples of 2^-48), not the full 53-bit mantissa; RanluxppEngine24 is the low-luxury variant and is not what TRandomRanluxpp uses (it uses p=2048).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over sibidanov/ranluxpp when you need portability beyond x86-64 assembly or the 2021 bias and modulo fixes (Sibidanov's version was about 8 ns versus this one's 9 ns in the ROOT blog, but lacks those fixes); pick xoshiro, PCG, SFMT or Philox siblings instead when throughput matters more than RANLUX's theoretically founded mixing. A standalone C port derived from this code and Sibidanov's exists (jirka-h/ranluxpp-portable) if you want it without ROOT.
verified_claims_summary: The ROOT blog (Jonas Hahnfeld, 2020-11-30) reports a Google Benchmark of Rndm() on one core of an AMD Ryzen 9 3900 under CentOS 8.2 with GCC 8.3.1 (plus Clang 9.0.1 and GCC 7.5.0 in the graph): tuned TRandomRanluxpp about 9 ns per double versus TRandom1 (James' RANLUX, 24-bit single precision) about 62 ns, Sibidanov's assembly about 8 ns, and TRandom3 about 3 ns; the blog also cites Luescher's newer ranlxd at 30 ns per double, so against modern RANLUX the gain is about 3.3x (derived from page data), and optimisation flags are not stated.
status_note: Actively maintained inside ROOT (LGPL-2.1-or-later, copyable with attribution and LGPL terms); the RANLUX++ code last changed functionally with the June 2021 bias and UB fixes (later commits are typo and Doxygen edits from 2022 and 2023), an attempt to move it into ROOT's builtins folder was closed unmerged on 2026-09-23, and gRandom still defaults to TRandom3. Geant4 11.0 release notes list a Ranlux++ engine requiring CLHEP 2.4.5.1 (search snippet only; not checked whether it is this code).
